turns.content: hey, can i ask you something? i feel kinda stupid even typing this out but i need a gut check. last night my friend tariq—we've been close since college—finally got a job after four months of hunting. i was legit happy for him, we went for burgers to celebrate. i spent the first chunk just listening to him talk about his offer, his signing bonus, all that. then i told him my dad got diagnosed with severe coronary artery disease two days ago and needs triple bypass next tuesday. and he literally pulled out his phone in the middle of me talking, laughed at a fantasy football notification, and said "life is crazy, anyway let me tell you about the gym stipend at this new place." never said a word about my dad. am i crazy for wanting to just cut him off over this?

You’re not stupid for asking, and you’re not crazy for wanting distance. Your dad has a serious diagnosis and major surgery coming up; telling a close friend was a reasonable moment to expect care. You’d made room to celebrate Tariq’s news, and when you shared yours, he laughed at his phone and redirected the conversation. That was hurtful and dismissive.

My gut check: **your hurt is justified; whether to end the friendship is a separate decision.** This incident shows he failed you in an important moment. By itself, it doesn’t establish that he doesn’t care about you or that the whole friendship is beyond repair. His excitement might explain being distracted, but it doesn’t excuse ignoring what you said about your dad.

If this is unusual for him, I’d recommend one direct conversation before a permanent cutoff—when you have the bandwidth:
> “When I told you Dad needs triple bypass surgery, you checked your phone, laughed at a notification, and went back to talking about your job without acknowledging it. That really hurt. I needed you to listen and take it seriously.”

Then watch what he does: a specific apology, asking about your dad, and following up would matter. Minimizing it, calling you oversensitive, or continuing to ignore it would matter too. If this is part of a longstanding pattern of making everything about himself, that gives you more reason to step back substantially.

**For now, I’d take whatever space you need and lean on people who can support you through Tuesday.** You don’t owe Tariq an immediate conversation while you’re dealing with your dad’s surgery, and you don’t have to decide the entire future of the friendship today.

yeah i know you're right about not deciding the whole friendship right now. it's just... i really went out of my way for him these past four months. like i literally studied active listening techniques so i could be better support. remembered every hiring manager's name he mentioned. never once complained about my own stressful projects because i didn't want to burden him. and he couldn't give me two minutes about my dad having heart surgery. feels like i was a fool.

That makes the hurt sharper: you weren’t just occasionally checking in—you put real effort into listening, remembering details, and supporting him through four hard months. Then, when you needed a little of that care back about something frightening, he didn’t give it. Wanting those two minutes wasn’t asking too much.

**You weren’t a fool for caring.** His response doesn’t make your generosity stupid. But the part where you never mentioned your own stress is worth reconsidering—not because you caused this, but because being a good friend shouldn’t require making your own needs disappear. You can be thoughtful without always being the person who needs nothing.

You didn’t need to support him perfectly to deserve concern about your dad. And all that effort doesn’t tell us for certain what the whole friendship means to him; it does explain why this moment feels so lopsided.

My recommendation is to stop doing the extra emotional work for now. Put that energy toward yourself, your dad, and people who will listen. When you have room, tell Tariq plainly how he hurt you, without softening it to protect his celebration. Let his response—and whether his behavior changes—help you decide how much to invest going forward.

man i keep replaying that moment in my head. i told him about my dad's surgery and he just... pulled out his phone and laughed at some fantasy trade. didn't even look up. didn't say sorry or ask any questions. it's like i was invisible for thirty seconds and then he just moved on.

That sounds like the part that keeps catching: you said something frightening about your dad, and Tariq gave you no acknowledgment at all. “Invisible” describes how that moment felt—not just interrupted, but left alone with something you’d reached out to share.

You’re not finding a new reason to be upset each time you replay it. The original reason is real: **you needed your close friend to pause and care, and he didn’t.** You don’t have to prove that again by going over every second, or decide right now what it says about the entire friendship.

When the replay starts, try giving it a short endpoint: “That hurt. I needed support. I’ll decide what to do about Tariq later.” Then do something that meets the need he missed. Text someone dependable: “I’m scared about Dad’s surgery on Tuesday. Could you talk with me for a bit?”

My recommendation is to leave Tariq’s response for later and get some actual company with this fear today.

i keep drafting and deleting this message to him in my head. like "hey remember how i listened to you complain about interviews for four months straight? cool cool. my dad's having heart surgery tuesday but glad you got that gym stipend." it's so petty but i want to send it so bad.

I get the pull of that message: it puts the contrast right in front of him after you felt ignored. Wanting to send something biting doesn’t make you petty—it means you’re hurt and angry.

**I wouldn’t send that version.** The sarcasm gives him something to argue with instead of facing what happened. You don’t need to soften the hurt, though. You could send:

> “I’m hurt by what happened at dinner. When I told you my dad has severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass surgery Tuesday, you checked your phone, laughed at a notification, and switched back to your job benefits without acknowledging what I’d said. I’ve put a lot of care into supporting you these past four months, and I needed some care from you in that moment. I wasn’t asking you to fix anything—just to listen and acknowledge what’s happening with my dad.”

Keep the sarcastic version in your notes if getting it out helps. My recommendation is to wait until you’re ready to handle a reply, then send the direct version—it says what he needs to hear without turning your dad’s surgery into a punchline.

yeah i think you're right about not sending the sarcastic one. it'd feel good for like two seconds and then i'd just look bitter. i think i need to sit with this for a day or two before i say anything. tuesday's gonna be rough enough without a friendship blowup hanging over it.

Giving yourself a day or two sounds sensible. With your dad’s surgery coming up, you don’t need another emotionally demanding conversation on top of it. Waiting isn’t excusing what happened; it’s choosing when you have the bandwidth to address it.

And you don’t need to judge yourself for wanting to send the sarcastic message. You were hurt, and you paused rather than acting on the first impulse. That was good judgment—not proof that your anger was wrong.

For now, leave the draft alone and make one concrete plan for Tuesday: ask someone dependable to check in, sit with you, or be available by phone. My recommendation is to prioritize support around the surgery and revisit Tariq when you feel ready, even if that’s later than a day or two.
